sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 -T3 --reason target -oA initial_assessment

Treat this as a general starting pattern, not a universal command. Choose parameters according to network capacity, assessment goals, and authorization scope.

docs.title: 1. Nmap Fundamentals
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Understand Nmap as a network exploration and security auditing tool without overstating what its results prove.

Nmap, or Network Mapper, is an open-source tool for network exploration and security auditing. It sends network probes and analyzes responses to report information such as reachable hosts, port states, services, versions, and, when conditions permit, operating-system fingerprints.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Nmap was released in 1997 by Gordon Lyon, also known as Fyodor. Over time, the project added capabilities such as service and version detection, OS detection, and the Nmap Scripting Engine. It runs on Linux, Windows, macOS, and other Unix-like systems.

docs.title: Primary use cases
docs.text:
Nmap is not limited to penetration testing. Common uses include:

  • Network inventory: Identify reachable hosts and exposed services.
  • Security auditing: Review network exposure and validate selected security controls.
  • Service validation: Identify services and versions listening on open ports.
  • Operations: Support upgrade planning, uptime checks, and network-access troubleshooting.
  • Authorized reconnaissance: Collect technical information before a security assessment.

Important limitation

Nmap infers results from network responses. Firewalls, NAT, proxies, rate limiting, packet loss, and non-standard host behavior can change or obscure the result.

docs.title: Conceptual architecture
docs.text:
Nmap capabilities can be understood as several functional areas:

  • Target specification: Define a host, network range, or target list.
  • Host discovery: Determine which hosts appear reachable using ARP, ICMP, TCP, and other probes.
  • Port scanning: Determine port states with different scan techniques.
  • Service and version detection: Send application-aware probes and compare responses with nmap-service-probes.
  • OS detection: Fingerprint TCP/IP stack behavior and compare it with nmap-os-db.
  • NSE: Run Lua scripts for discovery, version detection, and other security tasks.
  • Output: Save results in human-readable and machine-readable formats.

docs.title: Relationship with the TCP/IP stack
docs.text: Many advanced Nmap capabilities use raw packets. On Unix-like systems, some scan types therefore require privileged access. TCP Connect Scan is different because it uses the operating system's normal socket API and generally works without raw-packet privileges.

docs.title: Nmap in a security assessment
docs.text:
A common authorized assessment flow is:

  1. Define scope and targets correctly.
  2. Perform host discovery.
  3. Discover ports.
  4. Identify services and versions.
  5. Perform OS fingerprinting when conditions are suitable.
  6. Run selected NSE scripts after considering their side effects.
  7. Save and analyze the output.

This is a practical pattern, not a fixed requirement. Some networks require skipping host discovery, avoiding certain scan types, or lowering the scan rate.

docs.title: 2. Syntax and Command Structure
docs.text: Chapter goal: Build valid Nmap commands and avoid incompatible option combinations.

docs.title: General syntax
docs.text:
nmap [ <Scan Type> ... ] [ <Options> ] { <target specification> }
  • <Scan Type>: A port-scan technique such as -sS, -sT, or -sU.
  • <Options>: Host discovery, port selection, version detection, timing, output, and NSE settings.
  • <target specification>: An IP address, hostname, range, CIDR block, or target list.

docs.title: Option ordering
docs.text:
For many options, Nmap does not depend on a strict visual order. For readability, this documentation uses the following pattern:

  1. Scan type
  2. Host discovery
  3. Port specification
  4. Service or OS detection
  5. NSE
  6. Timing
  7. Output
  8. Target

Example:

sudo nmap -sS -Pn -p 22,80,443 -sV -T3 --reason -oA assessment 192.168.1.10

docs.title: Compatible and incompatible scan types
docs.text:
Do not assume that when two conflicting scan types are supplied, the last one automatically wins. Nmap accepts only supported combinations.

According to the Reference Guide, you normally select one TCP scan type per run. UDP Scan (-sU) and one SCTP scan can be combined with a TCP scan type.

Valid example:

sudo nmap -sS -sU -p T:22,80,443,U:53,161 192.168.1.10

For unsupported combinations, rely on Nmap's error output rather than a "last option wins" rule.

docs.title: Target specification
docs.text:
Common examples:

nmap 192.168.1.10

nmap 192.168.1.0/24

nmap 192.168.1.10-50

nmap example.com

nmap -iL targets.txt

docs.title: Practical combinations
docs.text:
Host discovery without a port scan:

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

TCP SYN scan of common ports:

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 100 192.168.1.10

Service detection with structured output:

sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 --reason 192.168.1.10 -oA service_assessment

docs.title: Common syntax mistakes
docs.text:
• Running raw-packet scans without sufficient privileges: On Unix, scans such as -sS and -sU generally require privileged access.
  • Combining options with conflicting intent: For example, -sn explicitly disables port scanning, so adding normal port-scan selection to the same task is usually meaningless.
  • Forgetting the target: Nmap needs a target or -iL input.
  • Using ranges incorrectly: 192.168.1.10-50 is valid, while ambiguous range notation can select unintended targets.
  • Omitting required arguments: Options such as -p, -oN, and --script-args need values.

About -p80

Nmap accepts compact forms such as -p80. This guide usually writes -p 80 for readability.

docs.title: 3. Host Discovery
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Identify reachable hosts before port scanning and choose discovery probes that fit the network environment.

Host discovery is the phase Nmap uses to determine which targets appear reachable. The exact discovery behavior depends on network type, privilege level, and selected options.

docs.title: -sn, no port scan
docs.text:
-sn tells Nmap to perform host discovery without continuing into a port scan.

nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24

On a local Ethernet network, Nmap normally prefers ARP discovery. On non-local networks, default probes depend on privilege level and can include ICMP and TCP probes.

Use case: Quickly inventory reachable systems without port scanning.

docs.title: -Pn, skip host discovery
docs.text:
With -Pn, Nmap treats every specified target as up and skips its normal host-discovery phase.

nmap -Pn 10.10.10.5

This is useful when discovery probes are filtered, but it can significantly increase scan time across large ranges.

Local-network behavior

On local Ethernet, Nmap can still use ARP to obtain MAC information. Use --disable-arp-ping, or --send-ip where appropriate, when ARP discovery must be avoided.

docs.title: -PE, ICMP Echo Request
docs.text:
Nmap sends ICMP Echo Request packets, Type 8, and an Echo Reply, Type 0, can indicate that the host is reachable.

nmap -PE 192.168.1.1

ICMP Echo is simple, but many environments filter it.

docs.title: -PP, ICMP Timestamp Request
docs.text:
nmap -PP 192.168.1.1

This uses ICMP Timestamp Request and Reply messages. Many modern systems do not answer them.

docs.title: -PM, ICMP Address Mask Request
docs.text:
nmap -PM 192.168.1.1

This probe is uncommon today and usually receives few responses.

docs.title: -PS <port list>, TCP SYN Ping
docs.text:
Nmap sends TCP SYN probes to selected ports. A SYN/ACK or RST response indicates that the host is reachable.

nmap -PS22,80,443 10.0.0.1

The port list follows -PS directly.

Use case: Discovery where ICMP is restricted but selected TCP ports remain reachable.

docs.title: -PA <port list>, TCP ACK Ping
docs.text:
Nmap sends a TCP ACK probe. A returned RST can indicate that the host is reachable.

nmap -PA22,80,443 10.0.0.1

This does not establish a full TCP connection. Results depend on firewall and routing behavior, so it should not be described as a guaranteed way to bypass a stateful firewall.

docs.title: -PR, ARP discovery
docs.text:
On local Ethernet, ARP is one of the most reliable discovery methods because hosts need ARP for IP communication within the same segment.

sudo nmap -PR 192.168.1.0/24

Controls such as port security, VLAN isolation, and network appliances can affect visibility, so calling ARP discovery "unfilterable" is inaccurate.

docs.title: --disable-arp-ping
docs.text:
This tells Nmap not to rely on ARP host discovery on the local network and to use selected IP-layer probes instead.

sudo nmap -sn --disable-arp-ping -PE 192.168.1.0/24

This is often slower or less reliable than ARP on a LAN, but it is useful when you specifically need to observe Layer 3 behavior.

docs.title: Choosing a discovery method
docs.text: Environment Good starting point Local LAN -sn with default ARP discovery Internet host with restricted ICMP -PS against expected reachable ports Hosts filtering discovery probes -Pn with a limited scope ICMP testing -PE, -PP, or -PM as needed

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Host Discovery

docs.title: 4. Port Specification
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Control exactly which ports Nmap examines and avoid unnecessary scanning.

By default, Nmap normally scans the 1,000 most common ports for each selected protocol. Port specification defines the port scope of a scan.

docs.title: -p <port ranges>
docs.text:
Specify one port, a list, a range, or a combination.

nmap -p 80 target

nmap -p 22,80,443 target

nmap -p 1-1000 target

nmap -p 22,80-100,443,8080 target

All ports from 1 through 65535:

nmap -p- target

Port zero is scanned only when it is explicitly requested.

docs.title: Protocol qualifiers
docs.text:
When scanning TCP and UDP together, use T: and U: to separate port lists.

sudo nmap -sS -sU -p U:53,111,137,T:22-25,80,443 target

Use S: for SCTP and P: for IP Protocol Scan.

docs.title: -F, Fast Scan
docs.text:
-F reduces the default set from 1,000 common ports to 100.

nmap -F target

It is faster, but services on less common ports can be missed.

docs.title: --top-ports <n>
docs.text:
Scan the n highest-frequency ports from nmap-services.

nmap --top-ports 200 target

For an initial assessment, this is often a better starting point than immediately scanning every port with -p-.

docs.title: --port-ratio <ratio>
docs.text:
Scan ports whose frequency ratio in nmap-services is greater than the supplied value. The ratio is between 0.0 and 1.0.

nmap --port-ratio 0.001 target

docs.title: --exclude-ports <port ranges>
docs.text:
Exclude selected ports from scanning.

nmap -p- --exclude-ports 25,110,143 target

This exclusion is not limited to port scanning and can also affect ports used for discovery.

docs.title: -r, sequential port order
docs.text:
Nmap randomizes port order by default. -r scans ports in numerical order.

nmap -r -p 1-1000 target

docs.title: Choosing an appropriate scope
docs.text:
Need Suggested option Quick inventory -F Initial assessment --top-ports 100 through --top-ports 1000 Specific services -p 22,80,443,... Full TCP review -p- with suitable timing Selected TCP and UDP Protocol qualifiers

Efficiency

A full-port scan is not automatically more professional. Define the assessment question first, then choose the smallest port scope that answers it.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Port Specification and Scan Order

docs.title: 5. Scan Types
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Choose a scan type based on protocol, privilege level, and the information required, rather than vague labels such as "invisible".

Most Nmap scan types use raw packets and require privileged access on Unix-like systems. According to the Reference Guide, unprivileged users normally rely on TCP Connect Scan and, historically, FTP Bounce Scan among the techniques covered here.

docs.title: -sS, TCP SYN Scan
docs.text:
Nmap sends a SYN packet:

  • SYN/ACK normally means open.
  • RST normally means closed.
  • No response after retries, or selected ICMP unreachable messages, normally leads to filtered.
sudo nmap -sS 10.10.10.10

SYN Scan does not complete the TCP handshake, so it generally creates fewer connection-level logs than Connect Scan. Modern IDS and IPS products can still detect it.

docs.title: -sT, TCP Connect Scan
docs.text:
This uses the operating system's connect() call to establish a TCP connection.

nmap -sT 192.168.1.1

It is suitable when raw-packet privileges are unavailable. Because the connection is completed, the target service is more likely to log it.

docs.title: -sS versus -sT
docs.text: Characteristic SYN Scan Connect Scan Raw-packet privilege Usually required Not required Full TCP handshake No Yes Nmap control over packets Greater Lower Chance of service-level connection logging Lower Higher

docs.title: -sU, UDP Scan
docs.text:
Nmap sends UDP probes. For selected well-known ports, it uses protocol-specific payloads.

  • A UDP response can indicate open.
  • ICMP Port Unreachable normally indicates closed.
  • No response often becomes open|filtered.
sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 50 192.168.1.1

UDP scanning is often slower than TCP scanning because of rate limiting and the absence of responses in many states.

docs.title: -sA, TCP ACK Scan
docs.text:
ACK Scan is useful for distinguishing filtered from unfiltered. It is not designed to determine whether a port is open or closed.

sudo nmap -sA -p 22,80,443 10.0.0.1

An RST normally means unfiltered. No response, or selected ICMP errors, normally means filtered.

docs.title: -sN, -sF, and -sX
docs.text:
These scans rely on TCP-stack behavior:

  • NULL (-sN): No flags are set.
  • FIN (-sF): FIN is set.
  • Xmas (-sX): FIN, PSH, and URG are set.
sudo nmap -sF 192.168.1.10

On compliant stacks, RST indicates closed, while no response can mean open|filtered. These techniques are not reliable on every operating system. Some implementations, including some Windows stacks, behave differently.

docs.title: -sY and -sZ, SCTP
docs.text:
• -sY: SCTP INIT Scan
  • -sZ: SCTP COOKIE ECHO Scan
sudo nmap -sY 192.168.1.1

These scans matter only where SCTP is part of the assessment scope.

docs.title: -sI, Idle Scan
docs.text:
Idle Scan uses a suitable zombie host and an IP ID side channel to infer the state of TCP ports on the target.

sudo nmap -sI zombie.example 10.10.10.10

Privileges and zombie requirements

Idle Scan uses raw packets and should be treated as a privileged scan. The zombie host must also meet specific technical conditions, such as predictable IP ID behavior and low traffic.

Idle Scan can separate the apparent scan source from the scanner, but it is not "undetectable" and is not always practical on modern networks.

docs.title: -sO, IP Protocol Scan
docs.text:
This scans IP protocol numbers instead of TCP or UDP ports.

sudo nmap -sO 192.168.1.1

It can identify support for IP-layer protocols such as ICMP or TCP.

docs.title: -b, FTP Bounce Scan
docs.text:
FTP Bounce is a legacy scan technique that uses vulnerable FTP servers to connect to a third-party host.

nmap -b ftp.example:21 target

The technique is deprecated in Nmap, and usable FTP servers are rare today.

docs.title: Choosing a scan type
docs.text: Goal Common choice TCP assessment with privileges -sS TCP assessment without raw-packet privileges -sT UDP -sU Filter-rule analysis -sA IP protocol inventory -sO

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Port Scanning Techniques

docs.title: 6. Service and Version Detection
docs.text: Chapter goal: Identify services and versions while understanding probes, intensity, and the limits of version detection.

docs.title: -sV
docs.text:
-sV enables version detection. After suitable ports are found, Nmap sends application-aware probes and compares responses against patterns in nmap-service-probes.

nmap -sV 192.168.1.10

Results can include a service name, product, version, extra information, device type, and CPE data.

Banner grabbing is only part of the process

Version detection is not limited to reading a banner. Nmap sends multiple probes and matches responses against signatures in nmap-service-probes.

docs.title: Accuracy and failure modes
docs.text:
Version detection is not definitive. Incorrect or missing identification can occur when:

  • A banner has been modified.
  • A custom service or proxy sits in the path.
  • The product has no suitable database signature.
  • A firewall or middlebox changes the response.
  • A service runs on an unusual port.

For important security decisions, confirm the result with additional evidence.

docs.title: --version-intensity <0-9>
docs.text:
Intensity controls how many probes with different rarity values are attempted.

nmap -sV --version-intensity 5 192.168.1.10
  • Lower values: Faster, with fewer probes.
  • Higher values: More probes and potentially better identification, at the cost of time.
  • Nmap's default intensity is 7.

Intensity zero

--version-intensity 0 does not mean that no probes are sent. Probes defined directly for a target port can still run regardless of the intensity value.

docs.title: --version-light
docs.text:
Alias for --version-intensity 2.

nmap -sV --version-light 192.168.1.0/24

Useful for faster inventory, with a lower chance of identifying uncommon services.

docs.title: --version-all
docs.text:
Alias for --version-intensity 9. It attempts all appropriate version-detection probes.

nmap -sV --version-all 192.168.1.10

docs.title: --allports
docs.text:
Nmap version detection normally excludes selected ports according to Exclude directives in nmap-service-probes. TCP/9100 is a well-known example because some printers print data sent to that port.

--allports tells version detection to ignore those exclusions.

nmap -sV --allports 192.168.1.10

Use with awareness

Probing ports that Nmap intentionally excludes can produce side effects on certain devices, especially printers.

docs.title: A controlled workflow
docs.text:
Start with port discovery:

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 200 192.168.1.10

Then run version detection on the ports you need:

nmap -sV -p 22,80,443,8080 192.168.1.10

This often provides better control than running intensive version detection across every port.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Service and Version Detection

docs.title: 7. OS Detection
docs.text: Chapter goal: Understand TCP/IP fingerprinting and report OS detection as a technical estimate, not an unquestionable fact.

docs.title: -O, OS Detection
docs.text:
Nmap sends a set of TCP, UDP, and ICMP probes and analyzes details such as TCP options, window size, IP ID behavior, and sequence characteristics. The resulting fingerprint is compared against nmap-os-db.

sudo nmap -O 10.10.10.10

This is active fingerprinting because Nmap sends traffic to create observable responses.

docs.title: What can the result contain?
docs.text:
Depending on match quality, Nmap can report:

  • Probable OS family and generation
  • Vendor
  • Device type
  • CPE
  • Confidence values for close guesses

docs.title: Conditions for better accuracy
docs.text:
OS detection generally works best when Nmap finds at least one open and one closed TCP port. That gives the fingerprinting engine a wider variety of responses.

Firewalls, NAT, load balancers, packet normalization, and customized TCP/IP stacks can change the fingerprint.

docs.title: --osscan-limit
docs.text:
This tells Nmap to attempt OS detection only against hosts whose conditions look promising, commonly hosts with at least one open and one closed port.

sudo nmap -O --osscan-limit 192.168.1.0/24

Across a large scope, this can reduce unnecessary time and traffic.

docs.title: --osscan-guess and --fuzzy
docs.text:
When there is no exact match, these options allow Nmap to display closer guesses with lower confidence.

sudo nmap -O --osscan-guess 192.168.1.100

Do not report a guess as a fact

If Nmap returns multiple matches with different confidence levels, describe them as probabilities. Confirm important conclusions with service banners, asset inventory, or other evidence.

docs.title: --max-os-tries
docs.text:
Controls the maximum number of OS-fingerprinting attempts.

sudo nmap -O --max-os-tries 1 192.168.1.100

Reducing the value can make scanning faster, but can also reduce the chance of obtaining a better match.

docs.title: Combining with version detection
docs.text:
Service detection and OS detection complement one another:

sudo nmap -sS -sV -O --top-ports 200 192.168.1.10

The -A option enables OS detection, version detection, and several additional capabilities, so review scope and impact before using it.

docs.title: Official references
docs.text:
• OS Detection
  • OS Detection Usage

docs.title: 8. NSE, Nmap Scripting Engine
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Use NSE in a controlled way by understanding script categories, arguments, and possible side effects.

The Nmap Scripting Engine, or NSE, runs Lua scripts for discovery, version detection, vulnerability checks, and other network tasks.

Scripts are not sandboxed

According to Nmap documentation, NSE scripts do not run in a security sandbox. Review source code and scope before running third-party scripts or scripts in categories such as intrusive, brute, exploit, and dos.

docs.title: NSE architecture
docs.text:
• Scripts: .nse files distributed with Nmap or added by the user.
  • Libraries: Lua modules in nselib.
  • Engine: The Nmap component that handles script rules, execution, and output.

docs.title: Important categories
docs.text:
Category General purpose auth Authentication and access-control checks broadcast Broadcast-based local-network discovery brute Credential guessing and brute force default Scripts selected by -sC or --script=default discovery Additional host and service information dos Denial-of-service-related checks or behavior exploit Exploitation-related scripts external Uses a third-party service or resource fuzzer Sends unusual input to test service behavior intrusive Higher-impact scripts or scripts producing significant traffic malware Checks for malware indicators safe Scripts designed to be lower risk version Complements version detection vuln Checks for known vulnerabilities

NSEDoc for a specific Nmap release can list additional categories. Always check the documentation matching the version you run.

docs.title: Running scripts
docs.text:
One script:

nmap --script http-title -p 80,443 target

A category:

nmap --script safe target

An expression:

nmap --script "http-* and not (brute or dos)" target

Default scripts:

nmap -sC target

-sC is equivalent to --script=default.

docs.title: --script-args
docs.text:
Passes arguments to scripts.

nmap --script http-headers --script-args http-headers.url=/admin target

Review each script's NSEDoc entry before supplying arguments.

docs.title: --script-help
docs.text:
Shows script documentation without running the script.

nmap --script-help ssh-hostkey

For an unfamiliar script, this should be one of the first commands you run.

docs.title: --script-updatedb
docs.text:
Refreshes the script database after adding or removing NSE scripts.

sudo nmap --script-updatedb

docs.title: 20 useful scripts
docs.text:
1. http-headers, displays HTTP headers.
  2. http-title, retrieves page titles.
  3. ssl-cert, inspects TLS certificates.
  4. vulners, queries vulnerability information using service and CPE data and an external service.
  5. smb-os-discovery, collects OS and SMB information.
  6. smb-vuln-ms17-010, checks for indicators associated with MS17-010.
  7. ftp-anon, checks anonymous FTP access.
  8. ssh-hostkey, retrieves SSH host keys.
  9. dns-brute, uses a wordlist to find likely subdomains.
  10. mysql-empty-password, checks for MySQL accounts with empty passwords.
  11. redis-info, collects Redis service information.
  12. http-sql-injection, spiders web pages and checks for SQL-injection indicators. It is intrusive.
  13. http-enum, checks common web paths and resources.
  14. broadcast-dhcp-discover, discovers DHCP servers on the local broadcast domain.
  15. snmp-info, collects SNMP information when access is available.
  16. rdp-enum-encryption, inspects RDP encryption configuration.
  17. vnc-info, collects VNC service information.
  18. http-csrf, checks web forms for CSRF indicators and belongs to intrusive/exploit/vuln categories.
  19. http-robots.txt, retrieves entries from /robots.txt.
  20. whois-ip, retrieves WHOIS information from external sources.

Examples:

nmap -sV --script http-headers -p 80,443 target
nmap --script ssl-cert -p 443 target
nmap --script smb-os-discovery -p 445 target
nmap --script ftp-anon -p 21 target
sudo nmap -sU -p 161 --script snmp-info target

External scripts and privacy

Scripts such as vulners and whois-ip contact external services. Review what information leaves your environment before using them.

docs.title: A professional NSE workflow
docs.text:
1. Find the script in NSEDoc.
  2. Review its categories and arguments.
  3. Determine whether it is external or intrusive.
  4. Re-check authorization and scope.
  5. Start against one limited host or service.
  6. Interpret output together with version detection and other evidence.

docs.title: Official references
docs.text:
• Nmap Scripting Engine
  • NSE Usage
  • NSEDoc

docs.title: 9. Firewall / IDS / IPS Evasion
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Understand fragmentation, spoofing, and packet-shaping options for authorized testing of network controls, including their real limitations.

Nmap provides options that change traffic shape, source information, and packet characteristics. These are not magic techniques for bypassing a firewall or IDS. Effectiveness depends on topology, middleboxes, routing, and scan type.

Scope and side effects

Use these techniques only in a lab or authorized assessment. Spoofing and decoys can attribute traffic to other hosts and create misleading security events.

docs.title: -f and --mtu, fragmentation
docs.text:
-f fragments selected raw-packet probes into smaller IP fragments. A primary use is testing reassembly and filtering behavior in network devices.

sudo nmap -sS -f 10.0.0.1

Custom fragment size:

sudo nmap -sS --mtu 24 10.0.0.1

The --mtu value must be a multiple of 8.

Limitations:

  • Many firewalls and IDS/IPS products reassemble fragments.
  • Some operating systems reassemble outgoing packets before transmission.
  • Version detection and NSE generally use normal sockets, so fragmentation does not normally apply to them.
  • Fragmentation increases packet count.

docs.title: -D, Decoy Scan
docs.text:
Decoys make the target observe probes that appear to come from multiple source addresses, with the real scanner mixed among them.

sudo nmap -sS -D decoy1,decoy2,ME 192.168.1.10

Nmap also supports RND:<n> for random IPv4 decoys.

Random decoys

Using addresses belonging to other organizations can create false logs and alerts. In a professional assessment, use only addresses that are in scope and under your control.

Decoys do not work with TCP Connect Scan or version detection, and large decoy sets can reduce performance or accuracy.

docs.title: -S, spoof source address
docs.text:
Sets the source IP address for raw packets.

sudo nmap -sS -S 192.0.2.50 -e eth0 -Pn 10.10.10.10

With true spoofing, replies normally return to the forged source, so the scanner receives little useful data unless routing and the test environment are specifically designed for the scenario. Nmap often also needs -e and -Pn in such cases.

docs.title: -e <interface>
docs.text:
Selects the send and receive interface.

sudo nmap -e eth0 -sS 10.10.10.10

Nmap usually chooses an interface automatically.

docs.title: -g and --source-port
docs.text:
Sets the source port for supported operations.

sudo nmap -sS --source-port 53 192.168.1.1

This is useful when testing weak firewall rules that trust traffic solely because it originates from a selected source port.

Important limitation: It does not control normal socket operations such as TCP Connect Scan, version detection, and many script scans. OS detection also needs specific source ports for some probes.

docs.title: --data-length
docs.text:
Adds random payload data to selected raw-packet probes.

sudo nmap -sS --data-length 64 10.0.0.1

This changes simple packet-size signatures but does not guarantee evasion against modern detection.

docs.title: --spoof-mac
docs.text:
Changes the source MAC address of raw Ethernet frames and enables --send-eth.

Random MAC:

sudo nmap -sS --spoof-mac 0 192.168.1.1

Vendor prefix:

sudo nmap -sS --spoof-mac Cisco 192.168.1.1

This affects raw-Ethernet capabilities such as SYN Scan or OS detection, not normal-socket version detection or NSE traffic.

docs.title: --ttl
docs.text:
Sets the IP TTL value.

sudo nmap -sS --ttl 128 10.10.10.10

Useful for labs, routing-behavior testing, or TTL-dependent policy checks. Changing TTL alone does not make a scanner anonymous.

docs.title: --badsum
docs.text:
Generates intentionally incorrect TCP, UDP, or SCTP checksums.

sudo nmap -sS --badsum 192.168.1.1

Normal host stacks drop packets with invalid checksums. A response can therefore indicate that a firewall or IDS processed the packet without full checksum validation.

docs.title: Limitations at a glance
docs.text: Option Main effect Important limitation -f, --mtu Raw-packet fragmentation Usually does not affect version detection or NSE -D Discovery, port scan, OS detection Does not work with Connect Scan or version detection -S Raw-packet source address Replies normally go to the forged address --source-port Selected raw scans Does not cover Connect/Version/NSE traffic --spoof-mac Raw Ethernet Relevant only in raw-Ethernet context --badsum Raw TCP/UDP/SCTP packets Mainly useful for observing middlebox behavior

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Firewall/IDS Evasion and Spoofing

docs.title: 10. Timing and Performance
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Control scan speed without unnecessarily sacrificing accuracy or generating uncontrolled network load.

Nmap adapts timing, parallelism, and retries based on network responses. The options in this chapter are useful when you have a defined time budget, network-capacity constraint, or assessment scope.

docs.title: Timing templates, -T0 through -T5
docs.text:
Templates adjust several timing parameters at once.

Template Name General use -T0 Paranoid Extremely slow, nearly serial probes -T1 Sneaky Very slow -T2 Polite Lower rate and network load -T3 Normal Default -T4 Aggressive Fast and reliable networks -T5 Insane Very aggressive timeouts, higher risk of missed results

-T0 applies a scan delay of roughly five minutes to selected probes, while -T1 uses roughly 15 seconds. -T2 also introduces substantial delay. These templates can make large scans take dramatically longer.

nmap -T3 target

On a reliable LAN:

nmap -T4 target

Lower rate does not guarantee stealth

Slower timing can reduce traffic rate, but it does not make a scan anonymous. Detection depends on sensors, signatures, retention, and overall traffic behavior.

docs.title: --min-rate and --max-rate
docs.text:
These control approximate packet-sending rates.

Limit the maximum rate:

sudo nmap -sS --max-rate 100 192.168.1.0/24

Force a minimum rate:

sudo nmap -sS --min-rate 100 192.168.1.0/24

--max-rate is useful for respecting network capacity or a change window. --min-rate can constrain Nmap's adaptive behavior and reduce accuracy on weak networks.

docs.title: --min-parallelism and --max-parallelism
docs.text:
These limit the number of outstanding probes.

sudo nmap -sS --max-parallelism 20 target

Nmap normally manages parallelism automatically. Override it only when you have a practical reason and measurements to support the change.

docs.title: --max-retries
docs.text:
Limits retransmissions for unanswered probes.

sudo nmap -sS --max-retries 2 target

Lower values make scans faster, but packet loss or rate limiting can create false negatives or more ambiguous states.

docs.title: --host-timeout <time>
docs.text:
Sets the maximum amount of time Nmap spends on one host.

nmap --host-timeout 10m target

Time values support units such as ms, s, m, and h.

docs.title: Practical choices
docs.text:
Stable internal network:

sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 -T4 target

Capacity-constrained network:

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 200 -T3 --max-rate 50 target

Defined per-host time budget:

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 1000 --host-timeout 5m --max-retries 2 target

docs.title: Professional principle
docs.text: Establish a baseline before changing several timing parameters at once. Changing one variable at a time makes it easier to understand whether improved speed or lost accuracy came from a specific option.

docs.title: Official references
docs.text:
• Timing and Performance
  • Timing Templates

docs.title: 11. Output and Reporting
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Store scan results in formats suitable for human review, automation, parsing, and reporting.

Nmap supports several output formats. Choose one based on who or what consumes the result: an analyst, automation pipeline, SIEM, parser, or final report.

docs.title: Interactive output
docs.text: The default terminal output includes scan results plus runtime information such as progress and selected alerts. It is not a separate file format.

docs.title: -oN <file>, Normal Output
docs.text:
Stores human-readable output in a file.

nmap -sS 192.168.1.1 -oN scan_results.nmap

Normal Output resembles terminal output but does not preserve every piece of interactive runtime information.

Good for: Manual review, report attachments, and simple archiving.

docs.title: -oX <file>, XML Output
docs.text:
XML is the most stable Nmap format for programmatic processing.

nmap -sS -sV 192.168.1.1 -oX scan_results.xml

Good for:

  • Parsers and automation
  • Import into other tools
  • Report generation
  • Structured scan archives

For new software integrations, the Nmap Reference Guide recommends XML over Grepable Output.

docs.title: -oG <file>, Grepable Output
docs.text:
This format places most host information on a single line, which is convenient for grep, awk, and shell tooling.

nmap -sS 192.168.1.0/24 -oG scan_results.gnmap

Deprecated

Grepable Output is deprecated. Use XML for new tools and pipelines.

docs.title: -oA <basename>, three major formats
docs.text:
Creates Normal, XML, and Grepable output using one basename.

nmap -sS -sV 192.168.1.1 -oA assessment

Files created:

assessment.nmap
assessment.xml
assessment.gnmap

-oA is practical when both manual review and parsing are required.

docs.title: --reason
docs.text:
Displays the reason Nmap assigned a host or port state.

sudo nmap -sS --reason 192.168.1.10

For example, a port can be marked open because of syn-ack or closed because of reset. This is valuable for troubleshooting and state analysis.

docs.title: --stats-every <time>
docs.text:
Prints periodic progress information during long scans.

sudo nmap -sS -p- --stats-every 30s target

docs.title: --append-output
docs.text:
Appends results instead of overwriting the destination file.

nmap target -oN history.nmap --append-output

Use care with XML because blindly appending multiple XML documents can create a file that parsers reject.

docs.title: Output to standard output
docs.text:
Use - as the filename to send a format to stdout.

nmap -oX - target

This is useful in pipelines.

docs.title: Recommended assessment pattern
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 --reason target -oA scans/initial

Choose filenames that identify scope, date, or assessment phase. This makes comparison and audit trails easier.

docs.title: Official reference
docs.text: • Nmap Output

docs.title: 12. Practical Scenarios
docs.text:
Chapter goal: Combine Nmap options into explainable and repeatable workflows for systems and networks you are authorized to assess.

Scope before command

Before running a scenario, confirm the target range, protocol, rate limit, approved testing window, and permitted test type.

docs.title: 1. Initial LAN inventory
docs.text:
Goal: Find reachable hosts without a port scan.

sudo nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 -oN network_discovery.nmap

On local Ethernet, Nmap normally uses ARP discovery.

docs.title: 2. Quick TCP assessment of one host
docs.text:
Goal: Check the 200 most common ports and save state reasons.

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 200 -T3 --reason 10.10.10.10 -oA quick_tcp

After open ports are found, run version detection only against the ports you need.

docs.title: 3. Targeted service and version detection
docs.text:
nmap -sV -p 22,80,443,8080 10.10.10.10 -oA service_versions

For a larger inventory with lower probe intensity:

nmap -sV --version-light -p 22,80,443,3389,8080 192.168.1.100-150 -oX service_scan.xml

docs.title: 4. Full TCP port review
docs.text:
Run full TCP port discovery separately from UDP and heavy NSE activity so troubleshooting remains clear.

sudo nmap -sS -p- -T3 --reason 192.168.1.50 -oA tcp_full

Then run version detection on open ports:

nmap -sV -p 22,80,443,8443 192.168.1.50 -oA tcp_services

docs.title: 5. Limited UDP assessment
docs.text:
Start with common UDP ports rather than all 65,535 ports.

sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 50 -T3 192.168.1.50 -oA udp_top50

Expand the port list according to expected services and assessment time.

docs.title: 6. Filter behavior with ACK Scan
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sA 203.0.113.1 -p 22,80,443 --reason

ACK Scan distinguishes filtered from unfiltered. It does not tell you whether a service is open or closed.

docs.title: 7. Rate-limited scan
docs.text:
For a change window or capacity-constrained network:

sudo nmap -sS --top-ports 1000 -T3 --max-rate 50 10.0.0.5 -oA rate_limited

Interpret the lower rate as load control, not guaranteed stealth.

docs.title: 8. Authorized web-service enumeration
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sS -sV -p 80,443,8080,8443 --script=http-title,http-headers,ssl-cert target.example -oA web_enum

Review documentation and scope before adding scripts such as http-enum or broader intrusive categories.

docs.title: 9. Specific vulnerability check after service validation
docs.text:
Example for SMB in a lab or explicitly authorized environment:

nmap -p 445 --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 192.168.1.20 -oN ms17_010_check.nmap

Using --script vuln across a large scope can trigger many scripts with different costs and behavior. A specific documented script gives better control.

docs.title: 10. Large network, two stages
docs.text:
Stage one: Host discovery and creation of a plain target list.

sudo nmap -sn -PE --min-rate 200 10.0.0.0/16 -oG - | awk '/Up$/{print $2}' > alive_hosts.txt

Stage two: Scan only the discovered hosts.

sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 500 -T3 --max-retries 2 -iL alive_hosts.txt -oA enterprise_scan

Why extract the addresses?

A raw .gnmap file is not a clean target list for -iL because each line contains extra fields. Extract addresses first or maintain a plain list.

docs.title: 11. OS detection for selected assets
docs.text:
sudo nmap -O --osscan-limit 10.10.10.1,10.10.10.100,10.10.10.200 -oN os_detection.nmap

OS detection is weaker when Nmap cannot find suitable open and closed TCP ports.

docs.title: 12. Output for automation
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 target -oX assessment.xml

Prefer XML over Grepable Output for new parsers and integrations.

docs.title: Pre-scan checklist
docs.text:
1. Scope and target ownership are confirmed.
  2. Scan type and privilege level are appropriate.
  3. Port scope is sufficient but not unnecessarily broad.
  4. Rate and timeout settings fit network capacity.
  5. NSE scripts have been reviewed for category and side effects.
  6. Output is saved for audit and analysis.

docs.text:

docs.title: 13. Output Analysis
docs.text: Chapter goal: Interpret port states and confidence without turning Nmap output into certainty or rushed prioritization.

docs.title: open
docs.text:
An application is accepting connections or packets on the port.

open does not by itself mean vulnerable. Service, version, configuration, exposure, and access controls must be assessed separately.

docs.title: closed
docs.text: The host is reachable, but no application is listening on the port. Closed ports can still provide useful information for host discovery or OS fingerprinting.

docs.title: filtered
docs.text: Nmap cannot determine whether the port is open or closed because a firewall, filter, or other network obstacle controls the probe or reply.

docs.title: unfiltered
docs.text: The port is reachable by the probe, but the scan type cannot determine whether it is open or closed. This is common with ACK Scan.

docs.title: open|filtered
docs.text: Nmap cannot distinguish between open and filtered. This occurs in scans where no reply has more than one possible interpretation, such as UDP and FIN/NULL/Xmas scans.

docs.title: closed|filtered
docs.text: In selected scan contexts, Nmap cannot distinguish closed from filtered. Check the scan type and reason rather than assuming one state.

docs.title: Use --reason for serious analysis
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sS --reason target

The reason identifies the packet or event behind a state, such as syn-ack, reset, or an ICMP unreachable response.

docs.title: False positive
docs.text:
A service or port is reported in a way that does not accurately represent the target.

Possible causes include:

  • Transparent proxies or load balancers
  • Middleboxes that generate replies
  • Service emulation
  • Customized banners or responses

docs.title: False negative
docs.text:
A service exists but is not found, or the state remains ambiguous.

Possible causes include:

  • Packet loss
  • Rate limiting
  • Firewall policy
  • Aggressive timeouts
  • Too few retries
  • Incomplete port scope

docs.title: Validation workflow
docs.text:
1. Review --reason.
  2. Repeat with more conservative timing where appropriate.
  3. Run service detection against the specific port.
  4. Use a protocol client such as curl, openssl s_client, or the service's administrative client when appropriate.
  5. Compare from another network vantage point if the assessment scope permits it.

docs.title: Security review priority
docs.text: Professional reports should prioritize security review rather than "attack priority".

docs.title: Higher priority
docs.text:
• Internet-facing services or services exposed outside their expected segment
  • Old or end-of-life versions
  • Management protocols such as SSH, RDP, SMB, or administrative web interfaces with inappropriate exposure
  • Confirmed weak authentication or anonymous access

docs.title: Medium priority
docs.text:
• Unknown or custom services
  • Unusual ports with incomplete version detection
  • filtered states that conflict with expected architecture

docs.title: Lower priority
docs.text:
• Closed ports
  • Known, patched services with appropriate exposure and access control

Final priority should consider asset criticality, exposure, authentication, version, and business context, not only port number.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
PORT    STATE     SERVICE  REASON
22/tcp  open      ssh      syn-ack
80/tcp  filtered  http     no-response
443/tcp open      https    syn-ack

Interpretation:

  • 22/tcp: A TCP handshake can begin. Next review the service/version and access policy.
  • 80/tcp: The state remains uncertain and a filter can be in the path.
  • 443/tcp: A service is reachable. Version detection and TLS configuration need separate review.

docs.title: 14. Common Mistakes
docs.text: Chapter goal: Avoid mistakes that produce incorrect conclusions, unnecessary scans, or operational problems.

docs.title: 1. Scanning without authorization
docs.text:
The most important mistake is scanning outside the approved scope or without permission.

Before execution, confirm:

  • Which IP addresses or domains are in scope?
  • Which protocols and ports are permitted?
  • Are intrusive NSE scripts allowed?
  • Is there a rate limit or approved testing window?
  • Where will output be stored?

docs.title: 2. Wrong assumptions about privileges and -sS
docs.text:
Do not assume that an explicitly requested privileged scan such as -sS silently falls back to -sT when raw-packet privileges are missing.

When Nmap chooses its default scan and raw-packet privileges are unavailable, it generally selects TCP Connect Scan instead of SYN Scan. If you explicitly request -sS, check the real Nmap error and output rather than relying on silent fallback.

docs.title: 3. Combining incompatible options
docs.text:
-sn means no port scan. Normal version detection with -sV therefore does not belong in the same workflow because it depends on service and port information.

Likewise, do not stack TCP scan types without checking compatibility.

docs.title: 4. Full-port scan without a reason
docs.text:
nmap -p- target

The command is valid, but it is not always the right starting point. For many inventories, --top-ports or a targeted port list is faster and easier to control.

docs.title: 5. Treating OS detection as definitive
docs.text:
-O produces an estimate. Firewalls, NAT, middleboxes, and the absence of suitable open and closed ports can reduce accuracy.

Record confidence and context in your report.

docs.title: 6. Treating open|filtered as open
docs.text: open|filtered means Nmap cannot distinguish the two states. Do not report the port as open unless another validation method confirms it.

docs.title: 7. Ignoring UDP
docs.text:
DNS, SNMP, DHCP, and many infrastructure protocols use UDP. A TCP-only assessment can miss important exposure.

At the same time, keep UDP scans targeted because they commonly take longer.

docs.title: 8. Aggressive use of -T5
docs.text:
-T5 uses very aggressive timeout values. On links with latency or loss, it can produce incomplete results.

For most stable networks, -T3, or -T4 where appropriate, is more predictable.

docs.title: 9. Reducing --max-retries without a baseline
docs.text:
Fewer retries make scanning faster, but packet loss and rate limiting can hide responses.

Compare a small sample before and after changing retry behavior.

docs.title: 10. Forcing parallelism and rate without a reason
docs.text:
Options such as --min-rate and --min-parallelism are not automatically optimizations. Nmap already uses adaptive timing.

Override adaptive behavior only with measurements and an operational reason.

docs.title: 11. Running broad NSE categories without review
docs.text:
nmap --script vuln target

This can run many scripts with different behavior and costs. In controlled assessments, specify the scripts you need and review their documentation first.

docs.title: 12. Ignoring --reason
docs.text:
A state has less context without its reason.

nmap --reason target

The reason helps show whether a state came from an RST, SYN/ACK, ICMP error, or no response.

docs.title: 13. Using Grepable Output for a new pipeline
docs.text:
-oG is deprecated. Use XML for new integrations.

nmap -sV target -oX scan.xml

docs.title: 14. Invalid target lists
docs.text: -iL expects a list of target specifications. Do not feed a raw .gnmap file directly to -iL without extracting the IP addresses.

docs.title: Final checklist
docs.text:
Before scanning:

  • Scope is confirmed.
  • Required privileges are available.
  • Targets and port lists are correct.
  • Timing fits the network.
  • NSE scripts have been reviewed.
  • Output is being saved.

After scanning:

  • Nmap warnings have been read.
  • State and reason have been interpreted together.
  • Important results have been validated using a second method.
  • Guesses and facts are clearly separated in the report.

docs.title: Legal considerations
docs.text: Computer-access and network-testing laws vary by jurisdiction and contract. Record written authorization, clear scope, and operational coordination before an assessment.

docs.title: Nmap Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick reference for common Nmap commands. Examples are intended for labs and authorized assessments.

docs.title: Targets and host discovery
docs.text: Goal Command Discover reachable hosts without port scan nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24 Treat all targets as up nmap -Pn 10.10.10.10 TCP SYN discovery on selected ports nmap -PS22,80,443 10.0.0.0/24 ARP discovery on a LAN nmap -PR 192.168.1.0/24

docs.title: Port selection
docs.text: Goal Command Selected ports nmap -p 22,80,443 target 100 common ports nmap -F target Top 200 ports nmap --top-ports 200 target All TCP ports nmap -p- target TCP and UDP with qualifiers nmap -sS -sU -p U:53,161,T:22,80,443 target

docs.title: Scan types
docs.text: Goal Command SYN Scan with privileges sudo nmap -sS target TCP Connect without raw-packet privilege nmap -sT target Common UDP ports sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 50 target Filter analysis with ACK sudo nmap -sA -p 22,80,443 target

docs.title: Service and OS detection
docs.text:
nmap -sV target

sudo nmap -O target

sudo nmap -sS -sV -O --top-ports 200 target

docs.title: NSE
docs.text:
Default scripts:

nmap -sC target

One script:

nmap --script http-title -p 80,443 target

Show script documentation:

nmap --script-help http-title

Review broad categories first

Run categories such as intrusive, brute, exploit, and dos only after reviewing script documentation and confirming authorization.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
nmap -T3 target

nmap -T4 --max-rate 100 target

-T3 is the default. -T4 is suited to fast, reliable networks. More aggressive values can reduce accuracy.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Human-readable output:

nmap target -oN scan.nmap

XML for software processing:

nmap -sV target -oX scan.xml

Three main formats at once:

nmap -sV target -oA assessment

Show state reasons:

nmap --reason target

docs.title: General initial-assessment pattern
docs.text:
sudo nmap -sS -sV --top-ports 200 -T3 --reason target -oA initial_assessment

This is a general starting pattern, not a universal command. Target type, network capacity, and authorization scope should determine scan parameters.

docs.title: Disclaimer and Authorized Use
docs.text:
This material is provided for education, documentation, and authorized security assessment.

Scanning third-party systems, networks, or services without explicit permission can conflict with law, organizational policy, or service terms.

Before running any scenario, define the approved assessment scope, testing window, scan rate, and target systems. In production environments, changing scan type or rate can affect services or network equipment.

The operator is responsible for obtaining authorization and complying with applicable rules and laws.

docs.text:
Use this page to choose a study sequence based on your experience and goal instead of reading every chapter linearly.

Guiding rule

Test every command in a lab or on a system you are explicitly authorized to assess.

docs.title: Content policy
docs.text:
When the original document conflicts with official Nmap documentation, the behavior documented by Nmap is the basis for this reference.

Terms such as "stealth", "fast", and "reliable" are not treated as absolute claims. Nmap results depend on scan type, privileges, the target system, firewalls, network quality, and timing parameters.

Review NSE scripts by category, documentation, and side effects before running them. Categories such as intrusive, brute, exploit, and dos are not suitable for unreviewed execution.

docs.title: Review status
docs.text: The professional edition aligns the core chapters with the Nmap Reference Guide and NSEDoc and corrects known errors from the initial document. For exact behavior of an option, the linked official documentation remains the final reference.
